newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China must wait for effects of HK return.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China must wait for effects of HK return.

text.p: For China, the midnight June 30 return of Hong Kong from British rule will redraw the national map, wipe out a century and a half of colonial humiliation and bolster the status of the world's most populous nation.

But while some of China's 1.2 billion people will be bleary-eyed from late-night festivities when they wake up on July 1, few will see any immediate difference in their lives from the end of 156 years of British empire in Hong Kong.

The mainland's already close economic ties with the colonial enclave on its southern coast and the political autonomy it has promised the territory mean the effects of reunion, while they may be profound, will take a long time to emerge, analysts say.

Britain's Union Jack flag will fly over Hong Kong until the formal midnight transfer of sovereignty, but in economic terms the colony returned to its ancestral motherland long ago, said Jason Kwok, chief China economist at Citibank NA in Hong Kong.
HONGKONG ECONOMY ALREADY PART OF CHINA
"The handover in July is irrelevant," Kwok said in a telephone interview. "Economically speaking, Hong Kong is already part of China... It's going to be business as usual."

China already benefited from Hong Kong's role as a conduit for foreign direct investment, equity investment and syndicated loans from abroad, a role that would continue to expand unaffected by Britain's imperial retreat, analysts said.

Hong Kong accounted for HK$624 billion ($80.6 billion) in investment in China in 1995. Total trade between the mainland and the territory -- most of which is bound for final markets further afield -- was worth over $40 billion last year.

While the handover would have little immediate impact on China, the long-term implications of unification with one of Asia's most sophisticated market economies were considerable, said Beijing-based analyst David Mahon of Mahon and Associates.
"To a great degree (China) will use Hong Kong as a paradigm of how it would like to develop large sectors of its own economy," Mahon said.
"I think on that level there will be considerable change, but it won't happen quickly -- at the earliest (after) 18 months, once the handover has begun to settle," he said.
CHINA TO LEARN FROM HONG KONG

While international interest focused on how Hong Kong would change after its return to China, there was every chance that the tiny territory of 6.4 million people would itself exert political and social influence on its huge motherland, said prominent U.S. analyst Kenneth Lieberthal.

"I think 10 to 20 years from now the issue is very likely to be more what was the role that Hong Kong played in the continuing changes in China," Lieberthal told a recent meeting of the Foreign Correspondents' Club in Beijing.

Freed from the embarrassment of emulating a Western-run rival, China would have the opportunity to learn not just from Hong Kong's sophisticated financial markets, but also from its highly-trained and effective civil service, he said.

"I think that expertise will be more widely available, and more trusted," Lieberthal said. "It will be much more legitimate to point to Hong Kong as part of China than it has ever been to point to Hong Kong as a British colony."

Would-be mainland reformers would be able to use Hong Kong as an example of how a free press, the rule of law, judiciary independence and tolerance for public dissent did not upset the successful functioning of a Chinese society, he said.
CHANGES WILL BE SLOW

More immediate changes wrought on China by Hong Kong's return are likely to be less dramatic, since Beijing has promised to accord the territory a high degree of autonomy for 50 years under its "One Country, Two Systems" formula.

Glowing predictions in state media of how the handover will boost inland provincial economies have been mingled with assurances that the distinction between mainland and territory will be scrupulously maintained.
National politics were likely to be little affected by Hong Kong, which will maintain its own government and financial and legal institutions, analysts said.

The example of limited democracy in Hong Kong could some day pose a challenge to the national grip on power of China's ruling Communist Party, but in the short term the handover's main significance was as a propaganda boost for Beijing, they said.
POSITIVE PUBLICITY, PATRIOTIC PROPAGANDA

Positive publicity from the end of the symbolic end of humiliation by foreign powers could help to counter the Party's loss of political controls and ideological legitimacy as nearly two decades of economic reform transform Chinese society.

"The leadership will be very keen to exploit the return, not only over the next couple of months, but well into the future," said one Western diplomat in Beijing. "It's easy to tap this sensitive nationalist nerve in the people."
Internationally, the return of Hong Kong will bring new foreign scrutiny of Beijing's policies from overseas governments and investors anxious about the territory's future.

Foreign and Chinese analysts agree that Beijing is determined not to suffer the embarrassment of failing to maintain Hong Kong's stability or prosperity, although questions remain on how well the mainland understands its prodigal son.

Ignorance of the realities of Hong Kong life was widespread in China, but Beijing had sent large numbers of officials to study the capitalist enclave and had gathered a body of expertise on its government institutions, said one diplomat.
SOURCE OF U.S. MISUNDERSTANDINGS?

The main post-handover danger was the possibility that Washington's eagerness to defend what it sees as essential liberties in Hong Kong would help to sour sensitive Sino-U.S. ties, said an analyst at an official Chinese think tank.
"If the United States applies its own value system to Hong Kong, then there will certainly be problems," said the analyst, who declined to be identified.

Some analysts argue that Hong Kong's harbour and defence facilities will be a major boost to the development of Chinese naval power in the South China Sea, where territorial disputes between Beijing and its South East Asian neighbours abound.
Chinese officials rush to scotch such suggestions by insisting that only the forces needed to defend Hong Kong itself will be stationed in the territory.
